note.explanation: A period is a horizontal row, and a group is a vertical column. The period tells the number of the shell being filled; the group helps identify how many electrons are in the outermost shell. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
examples: Group 17 has outermost-shell configuration ns² np⁵, so its elements are halogens.
Elements in groups 13 to 18 are p-block elements.
note.simple: Rows are periods; columns are groups. The row tells which shell is being filled, and the column helps tell the outer-shell electron pattern.
note.checkQuestion: What is the outermost-shell electronic configuration of group 17?
note.title: Reading periods, groups and blocks
steps: Find whether the element is described by a horizontal row or a vertical column.
Use the period number to identify the shell being filled.
Use the group’s outermost-shell configuration to identify its family and block.
note.answer: The periodic table has 7 periods and 18 groups. Groups 1 and 2 are s-block; groups 13 to 18 are p-block; groups 3 to 12 are d-block; and the two rows placed at the bottom are f-block elements.

options: The two rows placed below the table
mcqs.stem: What are the horizontal rows in the modern periodic table called?
rationales: This is correct because horizontal rows are called periods.
This is incorrect because vertical columns are called groups.
This is incorrect because the two separated rows at the bottom contain f-block elements.
This is incorrect because spaces between elements are not called periods.

mcqs.stem: How many periods are there in the modern periodic table?
rationales: This is correct because the modern periodic table has seven periods.
This is incorrect because there are seven periods, not eight.
This is incorrect because there are eighteen groups, not periods.
This is incorrect because 32 is the number of elements in each very long period.

mcqs.stem: What are the vertical columns in the periodic table called?
rationales: This is correct because the vertical columns are called groups.
This is incorrect because periods are horizontal rows.
This is incorrect because blocks classify elements by the subshell being filled.
This is incorrect because a family is another name for the elements present in a group.

mcqs.stem: Which outermost-shell configuration is shown for the halogen family?
rationales: This is incorrect because ns¹ is the configuration shown for group 1.
This is incorrect because ns² is the configuration shown for group 2.
This is correct because the table gives ns² np⁵ for group 17, the halogen family.
This is incorrect because ns² np⁶ is the configuration shown for group 18.

mcqs.stem: Which groups are called the p-block elements in this section?
rationales: This is incorrect because groups 1 and 2 are s-block elements.
This is incorrect because groups 3 to 12 are transition elements and form the d-block.
This is correct because elements in groups 13 to 18 are called p-block elements.
This is incorrect because the whole table is not the p-block.

mcqs.stem: Which two series are placed at the bottom of the periodic table because of the space problem?
rationales: This is correct because the lanthanides and actinides are placed in two rows at the bottom.
This is incorrect because these are families, not the two series placed at the bottom.
This is incorrect because neither name identifies the two separated series.
This is incorrect because these are group family names, not the two bottom series.

options: The number of shells being filled
The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of groups in the table
The family name of the element
mcqs.stem: According to Table (8.1), what does each period represent?
rationales: This is correct because each period represents the completion of a shell, and the table identifies the shell being filled.
This is incorrect because the period does not directly represent the proton count.
This is incorrect because there are eighteen groups in the table, not one per period.
This is incorrect because a family name is associated with a group.

mcqs.stem: Which groups are called transition elements in this section?
rationales: This is incorrect because groups 1 and 2 are normal elements and are in the s-block.
This is correct because groups 3 to 12 are called transition elements.
This is incorrect because groups 13 to 17 contain normal elements.
This is incorrect because group 18 is the noble-gas group.

written.text: The electronic configuration of the outermost shell of an element is s²p³. Find out period number and the group number of the element. In which block will you place this element?
written.finalAnswer: Group 15, p-block; the period cannot be fixed from s²p³ alone because the shell number is not given.

rubric.why: Counting the outermost electrons is the basis for identifying the group.
rubric.description: Identify the number of electrons in the stated outermost-shell configuration.
rubric.how: Add the electrons in s² and p³ to obtain five.

rubric.why: The group number is a requested part of the answer.
rubric.how: Use the group 15 configuration ns² np³ shown in Table (8.2).

rubric.why: The question also asks for the element's block.
rubric.how: The outermost configuration includes p electrons, so it belongs to the p-block.

rubric.why: The period depends on the number of the shell being filled, which is not shown in s²p³.
rubric.description: State the limitation in identifying the period from the given shorthand.
rubric.how: Explain that a principal shell number, such as 2 in 2s² 2p³, is needed to fix the period.

modelAnswer: The number of outermost electrons = 2 + 3 = 5.
The configuration ns² np³ belongs to group 15.
The p-subshell is being filled, so the element belongs to the p-block.
The shell number is not given in s²p³, so the period cannot be fixed from this information alone.

written.text: What is the group of the element having eight electrons in its outermost shell? In which physical state does this element exist?
written.finalAnswer: Group 18; it exists in the gaseous state.

rubric.why: The group identifies the family of the element.
rubric.how: Eight outermost electrons correspond to group 18 in the table.

rubric.why: The physical state is the second part of the question.
rubric.how: Group 18 elements are noble gases and exist in the gaseous state.

modelAnswer: An element with eight electrons in its outermost shell belongs to group 18.
It exists in the gaseous state.

written.text: An element belongs to 16th group and it is a gas. To which period does it belong?

rubric.why: Identifying the gaseous group 16 element leads to the correct period.
rubric.how: The gas in group 16 is oxygen.

rubric.why: The period is the requested final result.
rubric.how: Locate oxygen in the second period.

modelAnswer: The gas in group 16 is oxygen.

written.text: In which period and group will you place the element which is an important part of the solar cell? (a) Third period and 14th group (b) Second period and 14th group (c) Third period and 15th group (d) Third period and 16th group

rubric.why: The answer must identify the element's period and group.
rubric.how: Recognise the element as silicon and locate it in period 3, group 14.

rubric.why: The correct location earns the final mark.
rubric.how: Choose option (a), third period and 14th group.

modelAnswer: The element important in a solar cell is silicon.
Silicon is in the third period and 14th group.
Answer: (a) Third period and 14th group.

written.text: Identify the electronic configuration of the outermost shell of a transition metal. (a) ns²np⁴ (b) ndˣns² (c) ns²np⁶ (d) ns²np⁵

rubric.why: Recognising the transition-metal configuration identifies the correct option.
rubric.how: Use Table (8.2), which gives ndˣ ns² for transition metals.

rubric.why: The exact configuration is the required final answer.
rubric.how: Give ndˣ ns², option (b).

modelAnswer: The outermost-shell configuration of a transition metal is ndˣ ns².
Answer: (b) ndˣ ns².

written.text: Why does the size of a period increase as we move down the periodic table?
written.finalAnswer: As we move down, more shells are being filled and each shell has a fixed capacity for electrons; therefore, the number of elements in the periods increases.

rubric.why: The explanation must relate lower periods to shells being filled.
rubric.description: Mention the increase in shells being filled.
rubric.how: State that each lower period fills a shell with a larger capacity.

rubric.why: The fixed electron capacity explains why the period contains a particular number of elements.
rubric.description: Connect shell capacity to the number of elements.
rubric.how: Explain that a shell's fixed electron capacity determines the number of elements accommodated in the period.

modelAnswer: As we move down the periodic table, shells with greater electron capacity are being filled.
Since the number of electrons accommodated in a shell is fixed, the number of elements in the period is also fixed and increases for the larger shells.

written.text: In a group, the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell. Why is it so?
written.finalAnswer: Elements in a group have the same outermost-shell electronic configuration, so they have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell.

rubric.why: The answer needs to state the shared outermost-shell arrangement.
rubric.description: State that the elements share an outer-shell pattern.
rubric.how: Refer to their same outermost-shell electronic configuration.

rubric.why: This directly answers why the outermost electron counts match.
rubric.description: Link the shared configuration to the same electron count.
rubric.how: Explain that the same outermost-shell configuration gives the same number of outermost electrons.

modelAnswer: Elements present in a group have the same outermost-shell electronic configuration.
Therefore, they have the same number of electrons in their outermost shells.

written.text: How many blocks of elements are present in the periodic table? Are these blocks helpful in studying the properties of elements?
written.finalAnswer: There are four blocks: s, p, d and f. Yes, they are helpful because each block identifies the type of subshell being filled and helps in studying the properties of elements.

rubric.why: The number of blocks is explicitly asked.
rubric.how: State that there are four blocks.

rubric.why: Naming all blocks completes the classification.
rubric.how: List s, p, d and f.

rubric.why: The question asks whether blocks help in studying properties.
rubric.how: State that the blocks are helpful.

rubric.why: The reason explains what the blocks show about elements.
rubric.description: Give the reason for their usefulness.
rubric.how: Explain that blocks depend on the type of subshell being filled.

modelAnswer: There are four blocks of elements in the periodic table: s, p, d and f.
These blocks are helpful in studying the properties of elements.
The block depends upon the type of subshell which is being filled.
Answer: s-block, p-block, d-block and f-block.

written.text: Why do second and third periods have equal number of elements while all other periods contain different number of elements?
written.finalAnswer: The second and third periods each contain 8 elements, while the other periods contain 2, 18 or 32 elements because different shells have different fixed capacities for the electrons being accommodated.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the equal lengths of the second and third periods.
rubric.description: State the number of elements in each of these periods.
rubric.how: Give 8 elements in both the second and third periods.

rubric.why: The other period lengths demonstrate that period sizes differ.
rubric.how: Refer to the table: the first period has 2; the fourth and fifth have 18; the sixth and seventh have 32.

rubric.why: The explanation must connect period size with the shells being filled.
rubric.how: State that periods correspond to shells being filled.

rubric.why: Fixed shell capacity is the reason each period has its number of elements.
rubric.description: Explain why the number of elements varies.
rubric.how: State that the number of electrons accommodated in a shell is fixed, and shell capacities differ.

modelAnswer: The second and third periods each contain 8 elements.
The other periods contain 2, 18 or 32 elements, as shown in Table (8.1).
Each period represents the completion of a shell.
The number of electrons accommodated in a particular shell is fixed, and different shells have different capacities.

written.text: Modern periodic table is the amended form of the earlier table developed by Mandeleev. Elaborate how these two tables are different from each other.
written.finalAnswer: Mendeleev arranged elements in ascending order of their atomic masses, whereas the modern periodic table arranges elements in ascending order of their atomic numbers.

rubric.why: The difference in the basis of Mendeleev's arrangement must be stated.
rubric.how: State that Mendeleev arranged elements in ascending order of atomic masses.

rubric.why: The modern table's ordering is the key contrast.
rubric.how: State that the modern table arranges elements in ascending order of atomic numbers.

rubric.why: The comparison should make the difference between the two criteria clear.
rubric.description: Compare the two bases of arrangement.
rubric.how: Contrast atomic mass with atomic number.

rubric.why: The final answer should give the modern table's defining arrangement.
rubric.how: Conclude that the modern table uses atomic number rather than atomic mass.

modelAnswer: Mendeleev arranged elements in the ascending order of their atomic masses.
Later on, Moseley arranged the elements in ascending order of their atomic numbers.
Thus, Mendeleev's arrangement was based on atomic mass, while the modern periodic table is based on atomic number.
Answer: atomic masses in Mendeleev's table; atomic numbers in the modern periodic table.

examTips: A short question may ask for the definition of a period or group, the number of periods or groups, or the period and group of an element.
For a configuration question, show how the outer-shell electrons identify the group, then name the block from the subshell being filled.
For a question about periods, use Table (8.1): write the period, its number of elements and the shell being filled where relevant.
For a descriptive answer about blocks, name all four blocks and connect each to the subshell being filled.
Marks are easier to earn when the final response directly answers each part and includes the textbook terms: period, group, family, outermost shell and block.

explain.title: Periods
explain.body: The horizontal rows in the modern periodic table are called periods. There are seven periods in total. Each period represents the completion of a shell. Table (8.1) shows the number of elements and the shell being filled in each period.

explain.title: Groups and families
explain.body: The vertical columns present in the periodic table are called groups. There are eighteen groups. Elements present in a group resemble one another in their chemical properties since they contain the same number of electrons in their outermost shells. A group is also called a family.

explain.title: Group configurations
explain.body: Learn the outermost-shell configurations in Table (8.2). For example, group 1 is ns¹, group 2 is ns², group 17 is ns² np⁵, and group 18 is ns² np⁶.

explain.title: Blocks
explain.body: Elements are classified into s, p, d and f blocks depending upon the type of subshell which is being filled. Groups 1 and 2 are s-block; groups 13 to 18 are p-block; groups 3 to 12 are d-block; and the two rows at the bottom are f-block elements.

explain.title: Lanthanides and actinides
explain.body: The first series of fourteen elements starts after lanthanum and is called lanthanides. The second series starts after actinium and is called actinides. Together these two series are also called rare earths or f-block elements.

mistakes: Mixing up periods and groups: periods are horizontal rows, while groups are vertical columns.
Saying there are eighteen periods; the table has seven periods and eighteen groups.
Naming a block from the group number alone without checking which subshell is being filled.
Forgetting that the period depends on the number of the shell being filled; shorthand such as s²p³ does not itself show that shell number.
Calling the lanthanides and actinides groups instead of two series placed at the bottom of the table.
